title: Bandeja Paisa
subtitle: Colombian mixed plate with beans, rice, chicharron, chorizo and egg
excerpt: Colombia's most famous mixed plate: a generous spread of red beans, white rice, fried pork belly, chorizo, fried egg, avocado and plantain. This recipe serves 4 and takes about 2 hours to bring together. It is a meal that covers the whole plate and then some.
sourceNotes: Bandeja paisa originates from the Antioquia region of Colombia, the homeland of the paisas (people of the mountains). The dish grew from the high-calorie needs of farmers and labourers working the coffee and banana plantations. It is now considered the unofficial national dish of Colombia and is served in restaurants across the country and the Colombian diaspora.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The beans and hogao sauce can be made a day ahead. Fry the chicharron, chorizo, egg and plantain fresh to serve.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fried pork skin or belly that has been rendered until crispy. In Colombia it usually refers to fried pork belly pieces with the skin on, served as part of bandeja paisa and other regional dishes.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 2 hours from start to the table, with the beans requiring the most time. Bandeja paisa is less a single recipe than a collection of components cooked and served together. The key is timing: get the beans on first, then work through the rest while they simmer.

is the component that requires the most attention. Score the skin of the pork belly with a sharp knife and cook it slowly in its own fat, skin-side down, until the skin is deeply golden and the fat is rendered. Then flip and crisp the meat side. If you are short on time, shop-bought pork crackling makes a reasonable substitute, though the texture differs. The hogao sauce, a simple tomato and onion sofrito, ties the whole plate together.

items.prepNote: tin, drained, or 200g dried and cooked
pork belly with skin on, cut into strips

content.text: Cook the beans. If using tinned, heat them in a pan with half the onion, half the garlic, salt and a little water for 20 minutes until soft and well seasoned. If using dried beans, soak overnight and simmer for 1.5 hours. Make the hogao by frying the remaining onion and garlic in 1 tbsp oil for 5 minutes, then adding the tomatoes and cooking for a further 15 minutes until thick. Season with salt and cumin.
Cook the rice using your usual method or according to the packet. Keep warm.

Score the skin of the pork belly strips with a sharp knife. Heat a heavy frying pan over medium heat and place the pork strips in, skin-side down, with no added oil. Cook for 20 to 25 minutes, pressing occasionally, until the skin is deep golden and crisp and the fat has rendered out. Flip and cook for a further 5 minutes on the meat side. Season with salt. Drain on kitchen paper.

Slice 200g chorizo into rounds and fry in the same pan for 3 to 4 minutes each side until coloured. Remove and keep warm. Slice 1 ripe plantain and fry in a little oil over medium heat for 3 minutes each side until golden.
Fry the eggs in a little oil over medium heat, keeping the yolks runny.

Divide the rice and beans between 4 large plates. Arrange the chicharron strips, chorizo, fried egg, plantain and sliced avocado alongside. Spoon the hogao sauce over the beans. Serve with a corn arepa on the side if you have one.

attrs.symptom: Pork skin is not crisping up
attrs.cause: Heat too low or the skin is wet, which steams rather than fries
attrs.fix: Pat the pork skin very dry with kitchen paper before cooking. Use medium-high heat and press the skin flat against the pan with a spatula. Patience is essential; it takes 20 minutes or more.

attrs.symptom: Beans taste bland even after a long cook
attrs.cause: Under-seasoned or not enough aromatics added during cooking
attrs.fix: Season the beans generously with salt while they cook. Add more hogao sauce stirred through the beans just before serving. A pinch of cumin and a splash of the hogao oil make a big difference.

attrs.cause: Plantain was too ripe or cut too thin
attrs.fix: Use a plantain that is just yellow with a few black spots. Cut into rounds at least 1cm thick. Cook on medium heat rather than high to avoid burning before the inside heats through.

content.text: Bandeja paisa comes from the Andean coffee region of Colombia, where it was the daily meal of coffee pickers and farmers. Today it is served in restaurants across Colombia and wherever Colombians have settled abroad. The plate is famous for its size, covering most of the table in front of you. In Medellin and across Antioquia, ordering a bandeja paisa is as much a statement of regional identity as a meal.
